promptText: What is the key difference between monitoring and observability?
options: Monitoring and observability are two names for the exact same practice with no meaningful distinction

Monitoring watches a predefined, curated set of metrics and alerts against known thresholds; observability is the broader property of exposing enough structured, correlated data that an engineer can answer a novel question after the fact, about a failure mode nobody predicted
Monitoring only applies to databases, while observability only applies to LLM APIs
Observability requires no instrumentation at all, only log files
explanation: Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance; observability lets you reconstruct what happened for a question you never anticipated, which is exactly what a support-ticket-triage incident investigation needs.

promptText: What is the fourth pillar of observability that AI systems add beyond metrics, logs, and traces?
options: Billing records
Evaluation/quality scores attached to a specific trace, answering 'was this specific answer actually good, not just fast?'
Source code version control history
User interface screenshots
explanation: A classical service's trace tells you it succeeded in some duration, unambiguously; an LLM call can succeed in that classical sense while still being wrong, so evaluation scores must be carried as trace-attached data to correlate 'this trace was slow' with 'this trace was also wrong.'

promptText: What is cardinality in the context of metrics instrumentation?
options: The total number of requests a service can handle per second
The number of unique combinations of label/tag values a metric can take on; most metrics backends store one independent time series per unique combination
The size in bytes of a single log line
The number of spans contained in a single distributed trace
explanation: A metric tagged only by status has low cardinality (2 values); adding an unbounded field like user_id can push cardinality into the millions, which is why cardinality is treated as a hard engineering constraint, not a style preference.

promptText: What is the core difference between head-based and tail-based sampling?
options: Head-based sampling only works for HTTP requests, while tail-based sampling only works for gRPC requests

Head-based sampling decides whether to keep a trace at request start (e.g., a fixed random percentage); tail-based sampling defers the decision until the request finishes, keeping the trace only if some condition (error, high latency, bad eval score) is met
Tail-based sampling is always cheaper to implement than head-based sampling
Head-based sampling captures 100% of traces by definition
explanation: Tail-based sampling costs more because every span must be buffered until the keep/drop decision can be made, but it reliably captures the highest-value traces (errors, rare failures) instead of relying on chance.

promptText: Why is it safe to put a user_id or session_id on a trace span or log line, but unsafe to put it on a Micrometer metric tag?
options: Traces and logs are designed to handle unbounded per-event uniqueness (one record per request), while most metrics backends store one independent time series per unique tag combination, so an unbounded tag causes a cardinality explosion
There is no actual difference in safety; both are equally risky in either location
Trace storage is free while metrics storage always costs money
Metric tags are encrypted by default while trace attributes are not
explanation: This is the single most common cause of metrics-backend cardinality incidents in instrumented LLM applications: copying a high-cardinality field from a span attribute onto a Counter/Timer tag.

promptText: What problem did Google's Dapper paper (2010) solve that plain per-machine log files could not?
options: It introduced the first metrics dashboard visualization tool

It attached a shared trace ID (plus a parent-child span ID hierarchy) to a request as it moved through multiple services, letting engineers reassemble the entire request's journey as a tree instead of manually correlating log lines across machines
It replaced the need for any application-level instrumentation entirely
It solved the problem of storing logs cheaply at scale
explanation: Before Dapper's trace/span ID propagation, correlating a single user request across five machines by hand was hopeless; Zipkin and Jaeger later made this pattern broadly accessible as open source.

promptText: Why is tail-based sampling generally the better trade-off for AI pipelines, despite costing more to implement than head-based sampling?
options: Tail-based sampling never requires any buffering, unlike head-based sampling

The failures worth debugging in AI systems (hallucinations, tool errors, guardrail triggers) are rare; random head-based sampling captures a rare failure only with probability equal to the sampling rate per occurrence, requiring an enormous number of requests before capturing even one example, whereas tail-based sampling conditions the keep decision on the outcome itself
Tail-based sampling captures fewer traces overall, which reduces storage cost to zero
Head-based sampling is banned by the OpenTelemetry specification for GenAI workloads
explanation: At a true failure rate r and sampling rate p, you'd expect to need roughly 1/(r*p) requests before capturing one example via head-based sampling; tail-based sampling breaks this dependency by deciding after the outcome is known.

promptText: Why do 'orphaned spans' commonly occur across reactive or asynchronous boundaries (e.g., a Mono.subscribeOn hop) in a Spring WebFlux application?
options: Trace context is normally propagated via thread-local storage, which does not automatically survive a thread hop; if Reactor/Micrometer context propagation is missing or misconfigured, child spans exist but fail to correctly nest under their parent trace
Orphaned spans only occur when using a synchronous, blocking controller, never with reactive code
Spring WebFlux does not support distributed tracing under any configuration
Orphaned spans are caused exclusively by network partitions between microservices
explanation: This is one of the most common and confusing observability bugs in reactive Spring applications — explicit context propagation wiring is required to carry the trace context through the reactive pipeline across thread hops.

promptText: A metric is tagged by model (5 values), environment (3 values), and status (2 values), producing 30 time series. Someone adds a user_id tag with 2,000,000 distinct values. Why does the resulting series count become catastrophic rather than just large?
options: Because cardinality across independent tag dimensions multiplies rather than adds, so the new total becomes 5 x 3 x 2 x 2,000,000 = 60,000,000 series instead of a small additive increase
Because adding any new tag always doubles the total series count regardless of its own cardinality
Because Prometheus caps every metric at exactly 30 series and silently drops the rest
Because user_id tags are stored in a completely separate database with no effect on the existing series count
explanation: Series count is the product of each dimension's cardinality, not the sum; a single unbounded field multiplies the entire existing series count by its own cardinality, which is why an unbounded tag can bankrupt a metrics backend's index.

promptText: Why should a retrieval span in a RAG pipeline record retrieved-document identifiers and relevance scores rather than the full chunk text?
options: Full chunk text is technically impossible to attach to a span in any tracing system

Recording IDs and scores gives enough signal to diagnose whether retrieval surfaced relevant content, while avoiding the cost, storage bloat, and PII/confidentiality exposure of persisting full document text on every traced request
Relevance scores are legally required on every span by data protection regulations
Document identifiers are faster to compute than similarity scores, which is the only consideration that matters
explanation: This is a deliberate cost- and sensitivity-aware trade-off: IDs and scores are usually enough to tell whether a bad answer traces back to a bad retrieval, without paying the storage and exposure cost of full text on every request.

promptText: Why is '200 OK, low latency' insufficient evidence that an AI request was actually healthy?
options: 200 OK responses are always slower than error responses, so low latency alone is suspicious

Classical golden signals (status code, latency) say nothing about groundedness or correctness — a fast, well-formed, hallucinated answer looks identical to a fast, well-formed, correct one on every classical signal
HTTP status codes are deprecated and no longer meaningful for any modern API
Low latency responses are statistically guaranteed to be shorter and therefore less likely to hallucinate
explanation: This is why the evaluation/quality pillar must be attached to trace data — without it, a trace showing a fast, successful call gives no information about whether the content itself was trustworthy.

promptText: Why should PII/secret redaction happen in the OpenTelemetry collector pipeline before persistence, rather than only at the presentation/UI layer?
options: Redacting only at presentation (masking in the UI while storing raw text underneath) does not reduce actual data exposure risk, only its visibility — the sensitive data still exists in the backend store, accessible to anyone with direct data access
Collector-level redaction is required only because UI-level redaction is technically impossible to implement
Presentation-layer redaction is strictly more secure because it is closer to the end user
Redaction location has no security implication; both approaches are equivalent
explanation: A trace store that captures full unredacted text is functionally a second copy of sensitive data regardless of what the UI chooses to display, so redaction has to happen before export to any long-lived backend to actually reduce exposure.

promptText: A service handles 10,000,000 requests/day, and a full trace with prompt/completion text averages 8 KB. At a sampling rate of 1%, daily storage is about 800 MB. What happens if the team sets the sampling rate to 100% (trace everything at full fidelity), and what does this arithmetic imply for engineering practice?
options: Storage stays at 800 MB/day regardless of sampling rate, since sampling only affects query speed, not storage

Daily storage grows to roughly 80 GB/day, a 100x increase, which compounds into a large, expensive retention problem within weeks — meaning full-fidelity, unsampled tracing is a real, computable dollar-cost decision, not a default to leave untouched
Storage decreases at higher sampling rates because more data allows better compression ratios
The 8 KB average trace size becomes irrelevant once sampling rate exceeds 50%
explanation: Daily storage growth is N x p x s; scaling p from 0.01 to 1.0 scales storage linearly by 100x (800 MB to 80 GB/day), which is exactly the kind of explicit cost trade-off this chapter insists sampling rate should be, not an accident of default settings.

promptText: A customer complains that a support-triage agent recommended a refund policy that does not exist. The trace waterfall shows a retrieval span with top_score=0.83 (borderline relevance, 3 chunks used), a first model call with finish_reason=tool_calls, a tool span calling lookupRefundPolicy that took 98ms, and a second model call with finish_reason=stop. How should this trace be used to distinguish the possible root causes?
options: The trace cannot help distinguish root causes since it only records latency, not content

The borderline retrieval score suggests checking whether the retrieved chunks actually discussed the claimed policy (bad retrieval); the tool span's recorded return value should be checked against what the model actually stated (stale/wrong tool data); and if neither retrieved content nor the tool's return value supports the claim, the model likely fabricated it ungrounded by either source — the trace lets you check all three hypotheses directly instead of guessing
Since finish_reason=stop was returned, the answer is guaranteed to be correct and grounded
The 98ms tool latency alone proves the tool returned incorrect data
explanation: This is exactly the value observability provides over a single log line: the retrieved-chunk score and the tool's returned payload, both captured in the waterfall, let an engineer check whether the wrong policy came from bad retrieval, a stale tool response, or the model inventing something ungrounded by either, rather than guessing which of the three occurred.

promptText: Why must evaluation/quality scores be attached to the same trace ID as the request they judge, rather than stored in a separate, disconnected evaluation system?
options: Because trace IDs are required by law to accompany any stored evaluation score

Because attaching scores to the same trace ID is what makes 'which failures were also low-quality' a joinable query instead of a manual cross-reference exercise — without this linkage, a slow-or-erroring trace and a low-quality verdict for the same request cannot be correlated even if the evaluation runs asynchronously hours later
Because evaluation scores are only meaningful if computed synchronously within the same span as the model call
Because separate storage systems for traces and evaluation scores are technically incompatible with OpenTelemetry
explanation: This is exactly what distinguishes AI-aware observability from generic distributed tracing: the evaluation pillar has to be joinable to the same trace ID the request produced, even when scoring happens later as an async batch job, so quality and operational signals can be correlated for the same underlying request.
